coverageNote: Enumerated from disk: 7 units (domain root + 20.01..20.06) and 41 .md files — exactly matching the expected 7 units / 41 files. Every file was read in full through the 3a (implementer simulation) -> 3b (rubric scoring) -> 3c (devil's advocate) cycle; no sampling. Rubric dimensions 1 (Problem Clarity), 2 (Persona Specificity) and 6 (Competitive Positioning) are marked N/A for every unit: their artefacts are meta/problem-statement.md, meta/personas.md and meta/competitive-landscape.md, which sit outside this domain, and every unit correctly references personas rather than redefining them (20.01 index: 'Personas from meta/personas.md — referenced, never redefined'). Dimension 5 (Success Measurability) is N/A for six units for the same reason — product success metrics live in the vision meta layer, not in a domain folder — and applicable only to 20.06, which does assert a domain success metric ('alert->attendance conversion') in its own files. Dimensions 3, 4, 7, 8 are applicable everywhere and scored ✅ throughout except 20.06's dimension 7. Per scoring.md, implementer-simulation gaps are counted as additional checkpoints alongside the rubric dimensions; applicableCheckpoints per unit = applicable rubric dimensions + findings raised in that unit, and points = rubric points + 1 per blocking + 0.5 per warning. Aggregate: 6.0 points / 41 checkpoints = 14.6%. In 3c I dropped several candidate findings that did not survive attack: (a) the domain CX header count '13 High, 1 Medium' against a table carrying 12 High and 2 Medium — a factual slip with zero effect on what gets built; (b) roll-up Role Matrix mismatches between the domain index and sub-domain indexes (Operator on 20.05, Musician on 20.05.05) — roll-up summaries where the sub-domain matrix is authoritative and both cite the same tracked Q-04; (c) 20.04.01's Partial state describing a live product with no resolvable payout plan against 'a product reaching live without a bound plan is not a state the system can be in' — reconcilable as reach-live vs become-unresolvable-later; (d) bare `[PENDING]` cells in 20.01.05, 20.02.01, 20.02.02, 20.05.04 — each is substantively tracked by a well-formed Open Question row in the same file; (e) `[PENDING — /ideate-discover Step 5 deepening]` markers in 20.01, 20.03 and 20.04 CX files — well-formed per the tracked-deferral rule and legitimate while those leaves are still [PARTIAL]/[SURFACE]; (f) 20.05.03's Producer 'Reports (as split payee)' cell against D-03 'tips attach to the person' — D-03 is explicitly provisional pending its own Q-01, so the wider cell is correct. Note also that every finding below is about internal consistency; the tree's open-question hygiene is genuinely excellent — every one of the ~60 open questions I checked carries an owner and a deferral target, and resolved rows carry a citation to the resolving decision.

findings.claim: The `artist-asserted` consent-provenance tier is defined two incompatible ways: 20.01.02 calls it 'unmarketable-until-re-permissioned' (no marketing send at all) while 20.01.04 puts answered-provenance imports in a sendable warm-up tier that is merely throttled. Since D-08 coerces every owner-supplied consent event to `artist-asserted`, both rules describe the same records, and an implementer cannot tell whether an imported list can be emailed.
findings.evidence: 20.01.02-consent-legal-basis.md:88 — 'Owner-supplied import claims the strongest, platform-witnessed provenance to smuggle weak records into a strong tier | Downgraded to artist-asserted; the claimed strength is **rejected, never trusted** (CX-01). | Import completes; records land in the artist-asserted (unmarketable-until-re-permissioned) tier.' CONTRADICTS 20.01.04-fan-list-import-hygiene.md:45-46 — '4,335 created with provenance `artist-asserted: prior ESP double opt-in` / 5. Musician sees the breakdown and the consequence stated plainly: the new records enter a warm-up tier — first sends are throttled ([20.03.03]) because a cold blast to 4,335 unwitnessed addresses is how a sending domain gets blocklisted'. The same file also describes the same tier a third way at 20.01.02-consent-legal-basis.md:93 — 'the fan sits in the artist-asserted, deliverability-downgraded tier' — and at 20.01.02-consent-legal-basis.md:114 — 'this is why weak-provenance records are **throttled/tiered rather than trusted** (D-08 below)'. 20.01.04-fan-list-import-hygiene.md:93 reserves 'unmarketable' for a different trigger entirely: 'D-03 | Unanswered provenance imports data anyway, into an unmarketable tier'. 20.01-fan-graph-owned-audience-cx.md:41 records the underlying question as still open: '`[PENDING — /ideate-discover Step 5 deepening]` on whether weak-provenance records are sendable-with-warning or hard-blocked until re-permissioned.'
findings.failure_scenario: An artist imports 4,812 Mailchimp addresses and answers the provenance question ('Mailchimp double opt-in list, 2019–2025'). Implementer A follows 20.01.04's happy path and D-01 ('pricing that in with throttling rather than pretending otherwise') and lets the artist send a throttled warm-up campaign to all 4,335 new records. Implementer B follows 20.01.02:88 and marks the entire artist-asserted tier unmarketable until a re-permission campaign is run — but a re-permission campaign is itself a marketing send to those same records, so the list is permanently unsendable and 20.01.04's stated adoption gate ('an artist will not move here if their list cannot come with them') fails closed. The two builds differ on whether the domain's largest inbound cohort can be contacted at all.

findings.claim: 20.03.03 specifies a mandatory per-fan frequency-cap gate at dispatch and assigns ownership of the policy to sub-domain 20.02 — but no file in 20.02 (index, CX, or any of its three leaves) mentions frequency capping, fatigue, or a per-fan send budget. The only frequency policy in the domain is 20.01.03's fan-authored tier caps, which 20.03.03's own DT-04 explicitly distinguishes from this artist-blind budget, and which cannot express the per-day behaviour the edge case describes.
findings.forcedInvention: The implementer must invent the entire frequency-cap policy: its period (the UI copy implies per-day, the only existing cap is per-calendar-month), its value, who sets it (artist, platform, or fan), whether it is per-artist or global, and whether an over-limit message is deferred or dropped — none of which exists anywhere in the tree.
findings.evidence: 20.03.03-send-scheduling-throttling.md:61 — 'Two campaigns scheduled to overlapping segments in the same window | Both would buzz the same fan. A per-fan **frequency cap** (owned outside this node) governs: the second message is deferred or suppressed for the overlapping fans, not sent on top of the first. This node respects the cap; it does not own it. | "1,090 fans already got a message today — deferred for them."' 20.03.03-send-scheduling-throttling.md:93 — '**Gated by** per-fan **frequency capping** (owned in [20.02 Segmentation & Superfan Intelligence](../20.02-segmentation-superfan-intelligence/)) — this node checks the cap at dispatch and defers/suppresses over-limit fans (DT-04); it does not set the cap. `-cx.md` frequency-fatigue thread.' 20.03.03-send-scheduling-throttling.md:107 — 'D-08 | Frequency capping is a separate policy this node consumes, not owns'. A grep for 'frequency cap|frequency capping|fatigue' across the whole domain returns hits only in 20.03.03 (3) and 20.01.03:61 ('the tier\'s frequency cap is not already exhausted for the period') — zero hits anywhere under 20.02, and the named '`-cx.md` frequency-fatigue thread' does not exist in 20.03-broadcast-fan-messaging-cx.md, whose only cross-cuts are CX-01..CX-05 and R-01/R-02. 20.03.03-send-scheduling-throttling.md:81 (DT-04) explicitly rules out the 20.01.03 tiers as the same object: 'Throttling protects **shared platform reputation** (a fleet-wide ceiling, artist-blind); frequency capping protects **an individual fan from one artist\'s over-sending** (a per-fan, per-artist budget).'
findings.failure_scenario: An artist schedules a product-drop campaign and a tour campaign to overlapping Manchester segments in the same window. The dispatcher must consult 'the cap' — but 20.02 defines none, and 20.01.03's only cap is the fan-set Highlights tier of ≤1 marketing email per calendar month, which does not exist for the default 'All' tier. Implementer A concludes All-tier fans have no cap and sends both, producing exactly the double-buzz the edge case says must not happen. Implementer B invents a daily cap to satisfy the '1,090 fans already got a message today' copy and silently defers a tour announcement past its on-sale.

The stale claim is repeated without any marker in two 20.05 files.
findings.evidence: 20.03.02-channel-routing-bulk-delivery.md:40-44 — 'Push is only available where the fan has an app — and `meta/constraints.md` declares **web as the only surface**, with mobile an open question. Web push exists but is weak on iOS. This means push is, today, a channel this domain mostly cannot use.' CONTRADICTED by the same file at 20.03.02-channel-routing-bulk-delivery.md:119 — 'Q-04 | ~~Does DT-02 change the surface decision?~~ **RESOLVED** — yes... `meta/constraints.md` § Project Surfaces now declares **Mobile (PWA)** in **v1** ("web is installable as a PWA (home-screen, web push for gig alerts…)")... So push is not lost: it arrives in v1 as PWA web push'. The stale claim is restated with no marker at all in 20.05-memberships-patronage-campaigns-cx.md:83 — 'The go-live push is the one that matters, and it is the channel [20.03.02] DT-02 says the declared web surface cannot reliably deliver on iOS' — and 20.05.06-virtual-fan-events.md:99 — 'The go-live notification is the one that matters and it is the channel [20.03.02] DT-02 says the declared web surface cannot reliably deliver on iOS.'
findings.failure_scenario: A slice planner reads 20.03.02's Behavior and 20.05.06's Cross-Cut Notes and drops push from the v1 channel set for both broadcast routing and the livestream go-live notification, leaving email as the only channel — while 20.06.02 Q-01, 20.06 index Q-01 and D-28 all assume PWA web push ships in v1 as the gig-alert channel. The v1 fan-side alert product then has no push channel despite the ratified decision that it does.

findings.claim: 20.01.01 hard-disables marketing at record level for any fan record whose resolved keys are all unverified — which by its own key ranking is every import-only record — while 20.01.04's specified flow sends throttled warm-up marketing to exactly those records. This is a second, independent gate on the same question as #001 (identity verification rather than consent provenance) and neither file acknowledges the other.
findings.evidence: 20.01.01-unified-fan-record.md:80 — '**Partial data** — record exists but every resolved key is unverified (all guest/import) | Record renders; marketing send is **hard-disabled at the record level** until a stronger key verifies. | Explicit unverified badge, reduced contactability, "verify to enable marketing" affordance where applicable.' The key ranking that puts imports in that bucket is 20.01.01-unified-fan-record.md:36-39 — '**Resolution keys, strongest first**: platform account ID (exact, when the fan is logged in) → verified email (platform-witnessed a confirmed click) → payment-instrument fingerprint → **asserted email from import**.' CONTRADICTS 20.01.04-fan-list-import-hygiene.md:46 — 'the new records enter a warm-up tier — first sends are throttled ([20.03.03]) because a cold blast to 4,335 unwitnessed addresses is how a sending domain gets blocklisted' — a flow that presupposes those 4,335 import-only records are marketable. 20.01.04 never mentions identity verification of imported addresses anywhere, and 20.01.01:68 confirms an import onto an address with stronger existing provenance is a no-op ('Existing record wins; import is a no-op on that address'), so a pure import record carries only the weakest key.
findings.failure_scenario: The 4,335 records created in 20.01.04's happy path all have exactly one resolved key — an asserted email from import — so 20.01.01's rule marks every one of them marketing-hard-disabled. An implementer building the fan record enforces that gate and the artist's first campaign resolves to zero contactable recipients, while an implementer building only from 20.01.04 sends a throttled 4,335-recipient warm-up campaign. Nothing in either file states which gate wins, or what 'a stronger key verifies' means for an address the fan never clicked.

findings.claim: 20.01.02 defines a three-value consent purpose enum including `service`, and DT-04 requires a `service` message to carry its own grant, but no campaign purpose-type maps to `service`, no capture surface can produce a `service` grant, and 20.01.03's send-time resolution rule handles only `transactional` (always passes) and marketing (gated). The `service` purpose is unreachable and the implementer must invent what it is for.
findings.forcedInvention: What a `service` message is, which surface captures a `service` grant (the happy path captures only transactional + marketing; the preference centre exposes only channels, tiers and a global opt-out), and how a send resolves against a `service` grant given the campaign purpose-type enum has no `service` member.
findings.evidence: 20.01.02-consent-legal-basis.md:38-39 — 'which **purpose** it authorises (marketing, transactional, or service)'; 20.01.02-consent-legal-basis.md:23 — 'Selects, per channel (email / SMS / push), which purposes (marketing / transactional / service) they intend to rely on'; 20.01.02-consent-legal-basis.md:115 (DT-04) — 'A `marketing` grant does not imply a right to send `service` messages'. But the campaign-side enum has no such member: 20.01.03-fan-preference-centre.md:57 — 'each campaign carries a purpose-type — `transactional`, `general`, `release`, or `live-event-geo`, tagged by the sender at compose time', and its resolution rule at 20.01.03-fan-preference-centre.md:58-62 covers only two branches — '(1) `transactional` always passes... (2) marketing passes only if...' with 'A campaign left **untagged defaults to `general`**'. fanbase-direct-to-fan-cx.md:77 repeats the same four-value campaign enum. A grep for `service` as a purpose across the whole domain returns only the three 20.01.02 lines above.
findings.failure_scenario: An implementer building the consent ledger creates a (fan, entity, channel, purpose) tuple space with three purposes, then finds the preference centre can never write a `service` grant and the composer can never tag a `service` campaign — so every `service` tuple resolves to not-contactable forever. A second implementer drops `service` from the enum entirely, silently discarding DT-04's stated rule that a marketing grant does not license service messages, and later classifies a 'your membership renews Friday' message as `transactional` or `general` with no rule to decide which.

findings.claim: The domain CX file specifies that membership-gated vault items lock the instant a membership lapses and that the library must fail closed to locked, while 20.05.02 and 20.06.03 both specify the opposite as their shipping default — items released while the fan was paying stay accessible, and only future items lock.
findings.evidence: fanbase-direct-to-fan-cx.md:25 (CX-14 map row) — 'Membership-gated vault items ([20.05.02]) **lock the instant a membership lapses**, and that transition is **felt in the fan\'s library** ([20.06.03])' and fanbase-direct-to-fan-cx.md:356 (CX-14 §2) — 'Must be atomic-enough that the library never shows a stale *unlocked* state after a lapse — **fail-closed to locked on ambiguity**.' CONTRADICTS 20.05.02-exclusive-content-vault.md:73 — '`[PENDING — Q-01, user product decision]` — until ratified, **the safe default is no retroactive removal** (matches D-05); items opened while entitled stay accessible.' — and 20.06.03-fan-library-collection.md:120 — 'on lapse, per [20.05.02] DT-02\'s leaning, items **released while the fan was paying stay accessible** and future items lock. Locked items remain *listed* (greyed, `Renew to access`)'. 20.05.01-membership-tiers-benefits.md:78 restates the same interim default: 'so a lapsed fan keeps what they opened and loses only future items.'
findings.failure_scenario: A fan's card fails and their membership lapses on day 400. An implementer building the lifecycle from CX-14 fails closed and locks every membership-gated row in that fan's library, including a year of demos they opened while paying — precisely the 'a fan who loses a year of demos feels robbed' outcome 20.05.02 DT-02 is written to avoid. An implementer building from 20.05.02/20.06.03 keeps those rows accessible and locks only items posted after the lapse. Both cite a decision; the two libraries diverge for every lapsed member.

findings.claim: 20.06.03 specifies that a refund or chargeback revokes a digital entitlement and moves the item out of `Owned`, while 20.04.03 D-01 states the digital entitlement survives everything with an explicitly exhaustive single exception — a legal revocation order from domain 24 — which a refund is not.
findings.evidence: 20.06.03-fan-library-collection.md:128 — 'Payment later refunded / charged back after download | **Refund revokes the entitlement going forward**; the item leaves `Owned` and moves to a `Refunded` state (no longer playable in-app)... | Item shows `Refunded — access ended`; in-app playback stops'. CONTRADICTS 20.04.03-digital-sales-name-your-price-bundles.md:154 — 'D-01 | The digital entitlement survives everything | Physical fails, artist delists, pressing cancelled — the download stands. You cannot unhear a record, and trying poisons the one promise that separates buying from streaming. **Only a legal revocation order (domain 24) can override**, and that is not a storefront decision.' The same exhaustive framing appears at 20.04.03-digital-sales-name-your-price-bundles.md:96 ('Existing entitlements survive removal, always (D-01)') and is echoed at 20.06.03-fan-library-collection.md:176 — 'D-03 | Entitlements survive delisting, artist departure, and campaign failure'. 20.04.04-d2f-revenue-split-payout.md:113-114 specifies the money side of a refund/chargeback in detail and never mentions entitlement revocation.
findings.failure_scenario: A fan charges back a £20 NYP album purchase after downloading it. The entitlement store must decide: 20.06.03 revokes and stops in-app playback; 20.04.03 D-01 says only a domain-24 legal order can override, so the entitlement stands and the fan keeps a playable library item they were refunded for. Implementer A builds a revocation path the storefront spec says must not exist; implementer B builds a store where any chargeback yields a free permanent album.

findings.claim: The moment at which a sale binds its payout plan version is specified as payment settlement in 20.04.03 and, repeatedly and deliberately, as payment authorization in 20.04.04. These are distinct moments in a card flow and the divergence changes which split version pays a sale when a domain 09 dispute resolves mid-transaction.
findings.evidence: 20.04.03-digital-sales-name-your-price-bundles.md:108 — 'Split changes between add-to-cart and settlement (a dispute resolves mid-checkout) | The payout plan **version** is bound at **payment settlement**, not at add-to-cart, and the entitlement records that version.' — reinforced at 20.04.03-digital-sales-name-your-price-bundles.md:136 — 'the plan version bound at settlement. The seam is now display + plan-version binding at settlement.' CONTRADICTS 20.04.04-d2f-revenue-split-payout.md:115 — 'Prior sales pay the plan version live at their payment **authorization**; later sales pay the new. Each sale is locked to the split version live at the moment it is **authorized** — a domain 09 edit mid-checkout does not re-bind an in-flight sale.' — restated at 20.04.04-d2f-revenue-split-payout.md:99 ('Split applied at payment authorization against the plan version live at that instant'), :121 ('the accrual applies the split version that was live when the sale was authorized') and :82/D-11:178 ('plan version at payment authorization'). Both files are otherwise precise about payment moments — 20.04.03 also uses 'at payment settlement' for entitlement grant (:103) and atomic stock decrement (:101).
findings.failure_scenario: A fan authorizes a £15 NYP purchase; a domain 09 dispute resolves between authorization and settlement, changing the drummer's share from 10% to 5%. Under 20.04.04 the sale pays the pre-dispute plan (drummer £1.26); under 20.04.03 the entitlement records the post-settlement version (drummer £0.63). The payout engine cannot be built without picking one, and the two produce different money for a real payee on the same sale.

findings.claim: 20.02.03 D-03 states that an over-promise (eligible set larger than the presale allocation) is blocked at grant time, but the edge-case row for exactly that scenario offers the artist a second exit that is not narrowing the audience — declaring the presale first-come — which means the grant proceeds and the over-promise is disclosed rather than blocked.
findings.evidence: 20.02.03-perk-entitlements-presale-eligibility.md:96 — 'D-03 | **Over-promise is blocked at grant time** | See DT-02. Disappointing your best fans is the worst outcome this feature can produce, and it is entirely preventable.' CONTRADICTS 20.02.03-perk-entitlements-presale-eligibility.md:54 — 'Presale allocation smaller than the eligible set | **The most common real failure.** 1,203 eligible, 300 tickets... Must be caught at grant time, not at on-sale. | "You\'re promising 1,203 fans access to 300 tickets. Narrow the audience, **or say plainly that it\'s first-come**."' DT-02 at 20.02.03-perk-entitlements-presale-eligibility.md:76 asks for bluntness without resolving the question — 'The check must be at grant time, and it must be **blunt rather than a warning nobody reads**.'
findings.failure_scenario: An artist grants a 48-hour presale to a 1,203-fan segment against a 300-ticket allocation. Implementer A builds D-03 literally: the grant is refused until the artist narrows the segment below the allocation, and an artist who genuinely wants a first-come presale (a normal, legitimate pattern) cannot create one at all. Implementer B builds the edge-case copy: the grant proceeds behind an acknowledgement, so over-promising is permitted for anyone who clicks through — which is the 'warning nobody reads' DT-02 rejects.

findings.evidence: 20.04.01-storefront-product-catalog.md:43 — '| `physical-record` (vinyl/CD) | Held/pressed stock, ships | Finite; pre-order window allowed | **[20.04.02] + Q-03** | **Rights record (domain 09)** |'. CONTRADICTS 20.04.02-merch-variants-print-on-demand.md:115 — 'D-01 | **Merch splits are authored, never inherited from a recording** | See DT-02. The obvious implementation pays the wrong people.' — and its Role Lens at 20.04.02-merch-variants-print-on-demand.md:20 — 'Authors a merch split explicitly — **never inherited from a recording** (`-cx.md` CX-04)'. 20.04.02's declared scope includes pressings: 20.04.02-merch-variants-print-on-demand.md:10 — 'Physical merch: t-shirts in six sizes and three colours, posters, tote bags, **the limited pressing of 300**' — and its variant axes include vinyl at :48-49 ('occasional third axes (format for a vinyl variant colour...)'). 20.04-direct-to-fan-storefront-cx.md:113 states the merch rule absolutely: 'Merch has **no rights record** in domain 09 — there is nothing to reference. The split must be authored here'.
findings.failure_scenario: An artist lists a 300-copy vinyl pressing. Following 20.04.01's kind table, the catalogue binds the domain 09 rights record and the session drummer is paid 10% of every copy — the thesis working. Following 20.04.02, whose file owns `physical-record` detail and whose D-01 forbids inheriting a recording split, the implementer defaults the pressing to 100% to the listing entity and the drummer is paid nothing on the physical format while being paid on the identical digital release.

findings.failure_scenario: A downstream stage collecting unresolved [OWNER] questions by id from domain 20 reads '20.06.02 Q-04', matches the resolved row, and drops the live radius-reconciliation question — the one the file itself calls out as needing 'an explicit owner ruling on whether the two radii are one setting or two'. The 25 mi / 40 km alert radius and 20.01.03's 80 km / 50 mi preference radius then ship as two silently different settings that no stage was ever asked to reconcile.

findings.claim: The Segment Builder's dimension table names sub-domain 20.04 (Direct-to-Fan Storefront) as the source domain for the Membership dimension family. Membership tier, join date and lapse state are owned by 20.05.01; 20.04 has no membership concept at all, and 20.02.01's own Cross-Cut Notes never reference 20.05.
findings.evidence: 20.02.01-segment-builder.md:44 — '| **Membership** | tier / joined-since date / active vs lapsed (no activity in N days) | **20.04** |'. The actual owner is 20.05.01-membership-tiers-benefits.md:28 — 'What lives here is what a music membership *is*: a ladder of tiers, each granting entitlements' — and 20.05.01-membership-tiers-benefits.md:113 confirms the direction of the dependency: 'Feeds **[20.02.02 Superfan Score]** — tenure and active tier are strong signals.' 20.04-direct-to-fan-storefront-index.md:30-35 lists 20.04's four children (catalog, merch/POD, digital sales, revenue split) — none of them a membership. The adjacent rows in the same table cite their sources correctly ('19 Ticketing', 'CX-M13', '20.02.02, 20.03'), so this is not a shorthand convention.
findings.failure_scenario: An implementer building the segment builder follows the source column to 20.04 for the membership dimensions, finds no tier, join-date or lapse state in the storefront's four children, and either drops the Membership family from the builder — breaking CX-07 ('membership tenure and active tier are among the strongest superfan-score signals, and members are the single most obvious presale segment') — or invents a membership concept inside the storefront that duplicates 20.05.01.
